text: A maturity-based design for the integrated startup portfolio: DIC, Local Growth Acceleration, TASMU Accelerator, Scale Now and the MCIT Alumni Program
Reference: Enablement Programs Integrations Framework (September 2026)  |  Draft for management discussion  |  October 2026

The reference framework (MCIT Enablement Programs Integrations Framework, September 2026) gets the operating model broadly right: one section, one startup record, shared capabilities, common gates and an alumni loop. Its weakness is the program architecture underneath. Stages are defined by programs rather than by startup maturity, the gates test attributes that are easy to present and hard to verify, and the most consequential development step in a startup’s life — moving from early traction to product-market fit — has no clear owner.

This architecture rebuilds the portfolio from the startup outward. It starts with what must become true about a venture at each step, defines the evidence that proves it, and only then assigns programs. The result keeps all five reference propositions, but sharpens each one and changes how startups move between them.

Adopt a 10-stage Venture Maturity Model (M0–M9) as the single language for entry, exit, routing and reporting. Programs map to maturity bands; completing a program never moves a startup up a stage on its own.

Assess maturity on two axes: venture maturity and market position. An international company can be at repeatable growth at home but at market validation in Qatar. The reference framework conflates the two, which is why TASMU Soft Landing and Scale Now sit awkwardly in the same funnel.

Give Local Growth Acceleration one job: take startups from early traction to evidenced product-market fit and a first repeatable acquisition channel (M5 → M7). This closes the biggest gap in the current journey and removes its overlap with DIC.

Reposition DIC Pre-incubation as a light, high-volume, open-access track with no company-registration requirement. Requiring registration at ideation adds cost before the idea is tested, and conflicts with the reference entry gate that already asks for a validated problem.

Separate "completion", "graduation" and "qualification". Completion = finished the program. Graduation = met the program exit gate. Qualification = met the entry gate of a different program, assessed independently.

Make gate decisions independent of the program that delivered the support. Program leads present evidence; a Gate Panel with at least one external investor or operator decides Readiness and Scale gates. This removes the incentive to over-graduate.

Run investment readiness, market access/pilots, regulatory navigation and specialist technical support as cross-program services, not new programs. Each is needed at several stages, and turning them into programs would create more handovers and duplicate cohorts.

WHERE INSTITUTIONAL SUPPORT SHOULD STOP

From that point the relationship becomes an alumni and ecosystem relationship (give-back, policy input, deal flow) rather than a subsidy relationship. Scale Now is the last subsidised intervention, and it should be cost-shared.

text: Thesis: MCIT should increase the number of Qatar-anchored technology companies that reach repeatable growth and expand internationally. It does this by lowering the cost and time of generating credible evidence at each maturity step, while correcting specific market failures that private capital and markets will not correct on their own.

That makes the portfolio an evidence-generation system, not a training system. Every intervention exists to help a startup produce the next piece of decision-grade evidence (problem, solution, willingness to pay, retention, unit economics, repeatability, transferability to a new market) faster and more cheaply than it could alone.

text: 2.3 Where support begins and where it stops
Begins at M0, but at very low cost per founder. The aim at ideation is to grow the pool of capable founders and to filter cheaply, not to incubate ideas.

Intensity peaks at M5–M7. This is where the gap between "has customers" and "has a business" is widest, where failure is most expensive, and where public support has the clearest value (access to corporate and government buyers).
Stops at sustained M9, or earlier when private capital and customers already meet the startup’s needs. Continuing subsidies beyond this point crowds out private providers and ties up scarce capacity.
2.4 How the programs work as one portfolio
One maturity language. All programs use M0–M9, so a startup’s position is described the same way everywhere.
One front door, one assessment. A startup is placed by evidence, so direct entry at any stage is normal, not an exception.
Non-overlapping maturity bands. Each program owns a band. Where two programs touch a band (Local Growth and TASMU around M5–M7), they differ on the market axis, not the venture axis.
Shared services follow the startup. Capital readiness, market access, regulatory navigation and technical support are drawn on by any program when the startup’s maturity justifies it.
Independent gates. Moving between programs needs a separate qualification decision, so no program can push startups into the next one.

rows: Defined by what has been proven, not by time spent or programs completed.
Each stage has a primary evidence question. Evidence must be verifiable by a third party.
The gap between current evidence and the evidence the next stage needs.
Justified only if it closes that gap faster, cheaper or more credibly than the startup could alone, and the gap reflects a market failure.
A new piece of verified evidence that moves the startup up a stage, or an early, cheap "no" that frees founder time and public money.

PRINCIPLE
A fast, evidence-based "stop" or "pivot" is a valid portfolio outcome. A portfolio that only measures progression will push founders to fake progress.

text: The reference journey has six stages (Discover, Ideate, Incubate, Accelerate, Scale, Alumni). Four of these are named after programs and one (Alumni) is a relationship status, so the model describes where the startup is in MCIT, not how mature the startup is. The model below replaces it as the diagnostic layer. The reference stages remain as a simple communication layer for external use.

WHY TWO AXES MATTER
Without the market axis, an international company with US$m revenue and a Qatar-founded startup with ten customers both look like "acceleration stage". They need very different things. With two axes, TASMU Soft Landing is defined as "venture ≥ M6, Qatar market M2–M4" and Scale Now as "venture ≥ M7 in Qatar, target market M0–M2". The overlap disappears.

text: A startup is assessed at the highest stage for which all mandatory evidence is verified. Partial evidence for a higher stage is recorded as "emerging", but it does not change the stage.
Maturity can go down: a pivot to a new customer segment usually resets market evidence to M1–M2, while team and technical evidence carry over.
Maturity is reassessed at every gate and once a year for alumni. The startup record keeps the full history, so time-in-stage can be analysed.

Each stage is defined below. The "appropriate interventions" column shows what is justified at that stage, which may come from a program, a shared service, or an outside partner. Stage-to-program mapping is in Section 5.

ASSESSMENT INTEGRITY RULES
Revenue from shareholders, relatives, affiliated companies or grant bodies is excluded from commercial evidence.
LOIs count only if they name a price, volume or timeline. Unpriced LOIs count as M2 evidence only.
Recurring and one-off (consulting or project) revenue are reported separately; only recurring or repeat revenue counts toward M5 and above.

text: Place by evidence. Every applicant is assessed on both axes and placed at the program whose entry gate matches their verified maturity, whatever their history.

One program at a time for core programs. A startup can be enrolled in only one core program (Pre-incubation, Incubation, Local Growth, TASMU or Scale Now) at a time. Shared services can be used alongside.

Highest matching band wins. If a startup meets two entry gates, it is routed to the higher band, with targeted shared-service support for any gap. This stops a strong startup from being held back in an earlier program.

Residency limits. Each core program has a maximum residency (indicatively: Pre-incubation 3 months, Incubation 6–9 months plus at most one extension, Local Growth 6 months, TASMU 6 months, Scale Now 12 months including follow-up). Deep tech can have a documented extended plan.
